lesson.title: Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild
lesson.subtitle: The sixteen curated traps, embedded in context sentences

hook.title: The Minefield, Mapped
hook.content: The compendium keeps sixteen false friends — words that look like English and mean something else. Now that you can read German, they are the last real danger, because your guard is down. das Gift is poison (the present is das Geschenk). bekommen is GET (become is werden). der Chef is the BOSS (the cook is der Koch). fast means ALMOST (quick is schnell). bald means SOON (hairless is kahl). der Rat is ADVICE (the rodent is die Ratte). Sixteen traps, sixteen context sentences, zero excuses after today.

footnotes.title: Why False Friends Happen
footnotes.content: Sibling languages drift: Gift and gift both descend from 'a giving' — English kept the friendly branch, German the deadly dose (a 'gift' was once a dose of anything, including poison). False friends are true cognates with divergent stories — the drift is the history.

pattern.title: The Trap Walk
pattern.content: das Handy is the MOBILE PHONE (a German 1990s coinage — 'the handy thing in your hand'). aktuell means CURRENT (actual is tatsächlich). brav means WELL-BEHAVED (brave is mutig). die Fabrik is the FACTORY (fabric is der Stoff). das Gymnasium is the ACADEMIC HIGH SCHOOL (the gym is die Turnhalle). die Rente is the PENSION (apartment rent is die Miete). der Dom is the CATHEDRAL (a dome is die Kuppel). die Art is KIND/TYPE (art is die Kunst). eventuell means POSSIBLY (eventually is schließlich). die Kaution is the SECURITY DEPOSIT (caution is die Vorsicht). Read each in a sentence, feel the bite, remember the antidote.
pattern.linguist_note: bekommen vs become is the deepest trap: both are be + come, but English drifted the compound to 'turn into' while German kept 'come by, receive'. The word histories are identical — only the journeys differ.

exercises.prompt: Trap one: 'Ich bekomme ein Paket.' What happens?
exercises.explanation: The most famous trap in German: bekommen means receive. Becoming something is werden. And if the package were poison, you would say Mir ist übel — it goes badly with me.

exercises.prompt: Trap two: 'Das Kind ist heute brav.' What did the child do?
exercises.explanation: brav means obedient/good — the fearless child is mutig. A braves Kind is every parent's dream, no courage required.

exercises.prompt: Trap three: 'Ich bin fast fertig.' How far along are you?
exercises.explanation: fast da = almost there. Speed is schnell — another shift-family word you already own.

exercises.prompt: Trap four: 'Bis bald!' What are you promising?
options: See you SOON — bald means soon
exercises.target_answer: See you SOON — bald means soon
exercises.explanation: Bis bald = until soon. The hairless word is kahl. And eventuell means 'possibly' — eventually is schließlich.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.target_answer: Ich bekomme ein Geschenk für das Kind
exercises.meaning: I am getting a present for the child

vocab_hints.note: governs the accusative — für das Kind (kind = das Kind here, the child)
the SAFE gift — das Gift is poison!

exercises.explanation: Two traps dodged in one sentence: bekomme (get, not become) and Geschenk (present, not poison).
exercises.spoken: Ich bekomme ein Geschenk für das Kind
cues: Meaning: "I am getting a present for the child"
Opens with "Ich bekomme" and ends with "Kind".

summary.outcome: Identify all sixteen false friends in context and reach for the antidotes.

use_example.english: I am getting a present (not becoming one — and not a poison!).

summary.takeaway: False friends are true cognates with divergent stories — Gift/Gift, bekommen/become: know the drift, dodge the trap.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Whole-Trail Review Game — thirty topics, mixed modes, one last sprint.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild (I am getting a present for the child):
twist.target_answer: Ich bekomme ein Geschenk für das Kind
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich bekomme ein Geschenk für das Kind" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild without relying on short-term echo.

gift.context_translation: The poison is in the glass!
gift.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *giftiz 'a giving/dose' — the true twin of gift; German kept the deadly-dose branch. Trap: das Gift = POISON. (Present: das Geschenk.) [wiktionary]

bekommen.etymology_derivation: be- (by/around) + kommen (come) — literally 'come by (something)'; English become is the same be + come with a different job. [wiktionary]

chef.context_translation: The boss is in the office.
chef.etymology_derivation: The true twin of chief (both from Latin caput via French) — but German kept the workplace sense. Trap: der Chef = BOSS. (Cook: der Koch.) [wiktionary]

handy.etymology_derivation: A German pseudo-Anglicism from 'hand(y)' coined in the 1990s. Trap: das Handy = MOBILE PHONE, not 'useful'. [wiktionary]

aktuell.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin actualis — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: aktuell = CURRENT. (Actual: tatsächlich/wirklich.) [wiktionary]

rat.etymology_derivation: Ancient Germanic 'counsel' — the same root as 'read' (rædan, to advise!). Trap: der Rat = ADVICE. (Rodent: die Ratte.) [wiktionary]

brav.etymology_derivation: Both from Italian bravo — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: brav = WELL-BEHAVED. (Brave: mutig.) [wiktionary]

fast.etymology_derivation: Ancient Germanic 'firmly, almost' — true cognate of fast in its 'firm' sense. Trap: fast = ALMOST. (Quick: schnell.) [wiktionary]

bald.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *balþaz — kin to English bold; the 'daring' became 'soon'. Trap: bald = SOON. (Hairless: kahl.) [wiktionary]

übel.context_translation: I feel a bit sick today.
übel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *ubil — English evil is the documented cognate; both descend from the same ancient word for bad. [wiktionary]

melone.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian melone and Middle French melon, from Late Latin melo, short for Latin melopepo, from Greek; English melon is the same loan. [wiktionary]

still.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German stille, Proto-West Germanic *stillī; English still is the same word, and both kept the sense of motionless and silent. [wiktionary]

bluten.context_translation: The finger is bleeding a little.
bluten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bluoten, from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan, a verb from Blut. English bleed continues the same Proto-West Germanic verb. [wiktionary]

tablette.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French tablette, from the same French-Latin word family as English tablet; a pill pressed into a little tablet. [wiktionary]

brezel.context_phrase: Die Brezel ist ein klassisches Gebäck aus München.
brezel.context_translation: The pretzel is a classic pastry from Munich.
brezel.etymology_derivation: From Vulgar Latin brachiātellus, a little cake shaped like bent arms, from Latin bracchium, arm; English borrowed pretzel directly from German Brezel. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
